> **Accessible Component Pattern** — Architectural pattern for building WCAG 2.2 AA compliant UI components. Defines the five capability areas (semantic structure, ARIA, keyboard navigation, focus management, automated testing gate) that every interactive component must satisfy. For React-specific implementation steps, see [GUID-APP-ACC-001](../../../strategy/guidance/application/accessibility/GUID-APP-ACC-001-accessible-component-implementation-guidance.md).

[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

[STD-APP-ACC-001](../../../standards/application/accessibility/STD-APP-ACC-001-accessibility.md) mandates WCAG 2.2 AA compliance for all enterprise applications. Without a shared architectural pattern, teams independently attempt to satisfy these requirements, producing inconsistent accessibility behaviour across the component estate and repeated violations in production audits.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

The Accessible Component Pattern defines five capability areas that, when applied together, satisfy WCAG 2.2 AA requirements for interactive UI components:

1. **Semantic structure** — native HTML elements carry built-in accessibility semantics
2. **ARIA** — roles, states, and properties supplement native semantics where required
3. **Keyboard navigation** — all interactive functionality is operable without a pointer device
4. **Focus management** — focus position is predictable and controlled at all times
5. **Automated testing gate** — violations are detected and blocked in CI before deployment
page_texts.6:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#when-to-use-this-pattern]

### When to Use This Pattern

- Designing or reviewing any new component intended for end users
- Establishing accessibility compliance requirements for a new application or micro-frontend
- Evaluating whether a third-party component library meets the enterprise accessibility standard
- Defining acceptance criteria for an accessibility compliance milestone
page_texts.7:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- **Structural consistency**: All teams reason about accessibility using the same five-area framework
- **Shift-left quality**: The automated testing gate catches violations before they reach QA or production
- **Standard traceability**: Each capability area maps explicitly to STD-APP-ACC-001 requirements and WCAG 2.2 success criteria
- **Technology independence**: The pattern is framework-agnostic; implementation guidance for React is provided in GUID-APP-ACC-001

[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#business-context]

### Business Context

Healthcare applications at Gainwell serve users across a wide range of abilities — state agency staff, healthcare providers, and beneficiaries. Regulatory requirements (Section 508, ADA) and contractual obligations mandate accessible applications. Accessibility violations identified post-deployment are significantly more expensive to remediate than those caught during development.
page_texts.10:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

The enterprise component stack (per [ADR-APP-003](../../../decisions/application/ADR-APP-003-ui-component-system-selection.md)) uses **Radix UI** headless primitives, which provide WCAG-compliant keyboard navigation and ARIA roles by default. This pattern addresses the structural decisions that govern how components are built, regardless of the primitive library used.
page_texts.11:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Without this pattern:

- Teams satisfy WCAG requirements inconsistently — one team handles keyboard navigation; another does not
- Automated accessibility testing is not part of the definition of done, so violations are discovered in manual audits
- No shared vocabulary exists for discussing and reviewing the accessibility behaviour of a component
- Third-party component libraries are adopted without evaluating whether they satisfy the required capability areas

[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#pattern-overview]

### Pattern Overview

The Accessible Component Pattern structures all accessibility work into five capability areas. Each area maps to specific WCAG 2.2 success criteria and must be satisfied for a component to be considered compliant.

| Capability Area     | WCAG 2.2 Success Criteria          | Responsibility                              |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Semantic structure  | 1.3.1, 4.1.1, 4.1.2               | Developer — choose correct HTML element     |
| ARIA                | 4.1.2, 1.3.1, 1.3.5               | Developer — supplement semantics when needed |
| Keyboard navigation | 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.4.3, 2.4.7        | Library (Radix UI) or developer for custom  |
| Focus management    | 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 2.4.11, 2.4.13, 3.2.2 | Developer — manage explicit focus moves     |
| Automated testing   | All above                          | CI pipeline — axe-core gate                 |
page_texts.15:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#1-semantic-structure]

#### 1. Semantic Structure

A component's HTML element choice determines the accessibility semantics available to assistive technology. The pattern requires:

- Use the most semantically correct native HTML element available before applying ARIA
- Maintain a logical heading hierarchy within each page region
- Use list elements for groups of related navigational or data items
- Mark page regions with landmark roles (`<header>`, `<main>`, `<nav>`, `<footer>`)
page_texts.16:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#2-aria]

#### 2. ARIA

When native HTML semantics are insufficient, ARIA attributes supplement the accessibility tree. The pattern requires:

- Every form control is associated with a visible label
- Error messages are programmatically associated with their input via `aria-describedby`
- State changes that affect meaning are communicated via `aria-live` regions or role attributes (`aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-checked`)
- Purely decorative images and icons are hidden from the accessibility tree (`aria-hidden="true"`); images and icons that convey meaningful information must include descriptive `alt` text that clearly communicates their purpose to users relying on assistive technologies
- Custom interactive widgets explicitly declare their role, expose their current state, and dynamically update that state as users interact with them (e.g., an accordion toggle announces `aria-expanded="true"` or `aria-expanded="false"` when activated)
page_texts.17:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#3-keyboard-navigation]

#### 3. Keyboard Navigation

All interactive elements must be fully accessible via keyboard, ensuring users can navigate and interact without a mouse. Commonly accepted keyboard patterns must be followed (e.g., arrow keys for menus and radio groups, Enter/Space for buttons), and custom shortcuts must not conflict with standard browser or assistive technology shortcuts. The pattern requires:

- All interactive elements are reachable in a logical tab order via Tab (forward) and Shift+Tab (backward), with clearly visible focus states indicating the currently active element
- Composite widgets (menus, tabs, toolbars, listboxes) use roving `tabIndex` with arrow key navigation internally
- Escape dismisses modals, drawers, popovers, and menus
- Enter and Space activate buttons and toggle controls
- A "Skip to main content" link is the first focusable element on every page: visible on focus and hidden otherwise, it jumps directly to the main landmark (`<main>`) to allow bypass of repeated navigation
page_texts.18:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#4-focus-management]

#### 4. Focus Management

Focus position remains predictable when the DOM changes. The pattern requires:

- Dialogs and modals trap focus within their bounds while open
- Focus returns to the trigger element when a dialog, popover, or menu closes
- Client-side route changes move focus to the page's main heading or main content region
- No content receives `tabIndex` values greater than 0
- The focused element must not be completely covered by other content when navigating by keyboard
- Focus indicators must be at least as large as the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the unfocused component
- Focus indicators must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states
page_texts.19:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#5-automated-testing-gate]

#### 5. Automated Testing Gate

Accessibility violations are detected in CI before the component reaches a shared environment. The pattern requires:

- Every component has an axe-core unit test that asserts zero violations
- Page-level Playwright E2E tests run axe-core against interactive states (default load, error state, post-submission)
- The CI pipeline fails the build on any axe-core violation
- Tests target WCAG 2.2 AA rules (`wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag22aa` axe-core tags)

page_texts.20:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#pattern-structure]

## Pattern Structure

```
Accessible Component
├── Semantic Structure
│   ├── Correct HTML element (button, input, nav, etc.)
│   ├── Landmark regions (header, main, footer)
│   └── Heading hierarchy (h1 → h2 → h3, no skips)
│
├── ARIA Layer
│   ├── Label association (htmlFor / aria-labelledby)
│   ├── Error association (aria-describedby + role="alert")
│   ├── State attributes (aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked)
│   └── Live regions (aria-live="polite" / "assertive")
│
├── Keyboard Navigation
│   ├── Tab order (natural DOM order; tabIndex={-1} for programmatic focus only)
│   ├── Roving tabIndex (composite widgets)
│   ├── Standard key bindings (Enter/Space = activate; Escape = dismiss; Arrow keys = navigate)
│   └── Skip link (first focusable element on every page)
│
├── Focus Management
│   ├── Focus trap (dialogs, modals)
│   ├── Focus restoration (on dismiss/close)
│   └── Route change focus (move to main content on navigation)
│
└── Automated Testing Gate
    ├── axe-core unit test (per component, zero violations)
    ├── axe-core E2E test (per page, WCAG 2.2 AA tags)
    └── CI pipeline failure on violation
```

### Standards Alignment

This pattern implements [STD-APP-ACC-001](../../../standards/application/accessibility/STD-APP-ACC-001-accessibility.md). The capability areas map directly to the standard's sections:

| Pattern Capability  | STD-APP-ACC-001 Section |
| ------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Semantic structure  | §3.1                    |
| ARIA                | §3.2                    |
| Keyboard navigation | §3.3                    |
| Focus management    | §3.4                    |
| Automated testing   | §5.1                    |
page_texts.23:
[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#acceptance-criteria]

### Acceptance Criteria

A component satisfies this pattern when:

- [ ] It uses the most semantically correct HTML element for its role
- [ ] All form controls have an associated label; errors are associated via `aria-describedby`
- [ ] All interactive states are communicated via ARIA attributes
- [ ] All functionality is operable without a pointer device
- [ ] Focus is trapped within dialogs and restored to the trigger on close
- [ ] A skip link is present on every page-level layout
- [ ] An axe-core unit test passes with zero violations
- [ ] axe-core E2E tests pass with `wcag22aa` tags against all interactive states

[patterns/application/frontend/PTN-APP-FE-001-accessible-component-pattern.md#tldr]

## TL;DR

1. Every interactive component must satisfy five capability areas: semantic structure, ARIA, keyboard navigation, focus management, and automated testing
2. Use the most semantically correct HTML element; reach for ARIA only when no native element exists
3. Every page-level layout needs a skip link as the first focusable element
4. Dialogs trap focus; focus returns to the trigger on close
5. An axe-core test with zero violations is required for every component and every page state — violations block CI
6. For React/Radix UI implementation steps, see [GUID-APP-ACC-001](../../../strategy/guidance/application/accessibility/GUID-APP-ACC-001-accessible-component-implementation-guidance.md)
